title: The turning qiblah
hook: at the mosque of the two qiblahs, the prayer turns mid-way from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:144)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the charter of Medina, the city's clans named one by one. Your line was: one community of many. Who did you make sure was on the list? Day seven hundred seventy-five.

A row of people, bowed in prayer, and a voice at the door. Bukhari tells it like this. A man who had just prayed with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks past another mosque where people are in the middle of their prayer, bent over, facing toward Jerusalem. And he calls out: I bear witness that I have just prayed with the Messenger of Allah facing Mecca. And they turn. Right there, in the middle of the prayer, as they are. Today: the turning qiblah.
screen: `A VOICE AT THE DOOR.` → `FACING JERUSALEM.` → `THEY TURN, AS THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: The qiblah is the direction Muslims face in prayer. In Medina, the early Muslims had been praying toward Jerusalem. Bukhari says the Prophet loved that his qiblah would be the Ka'bah in Mecca, the house tradition says Abraham raised. And the Qur'an, in surah two, speaks of the turning of his face toward heaven, as if waiting. Then the verse comes. In Pickthall's words, in surah two, verse one hundred forty-four: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." The same verse says the believers too, wherever they are, are to turn their faces toward it. Now go back to that mosque. The news arrives mid-prayer. Nobody stops to hold a meeting. Nobody says, let's finish this one the old way and start fresh tomorrow. They turn, in the rows, as they are. Bukhari has a second report of the people of Quba hearing it at the dawn prayer and doing the same. Tradition remembers one of these places as the mosque of the two qiblahs, a mosque where a single prayer was offered facing two directions. Then there's the prayer itself. Its first half wasn't wrong. It was prayed in obedience, facing where they'd been told. The second half was too. What made both halves one prayer was not the direction. It was the turning: being ready to change where you face the moment the call comes, without leaving the prayer.
screen: `THE DIRECTION OF PRAYER.` · `HIS FACE TURNED TOWARD HEAVEN.` · `THE VERSE: TURN THY FACE.` · `ONE PRAYER, TWO DIRECTIONS.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: face the qiblah with fresh eyes. If you know where Mecca lies from where you're sitting, turn gently toward it now. If you don't, simply choose to sit facing one direction on purpose. Settle, and breathe. Notice that your whole body is pointed somewhere. Then think of one thing in your day you've been facing out of habit, and ask whether it's time to turn. Not to throw away what came before. Just to turn. If you pray, you can ask Allah to keep your face toward Him. Stay facing. The bell holds the time.
The turning qiblah. The day the direction of prayer changed from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah in Mecca, and worshipers turned in the middle of their prayer. Today's word.
Your line: turn to the house. Today, when you notice you're facing the wrong way in something, turn right there, mid-way, without waiting to start over. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'bah in Mecca for every prayer, wherever they are, and a mosque's niche (mihrab) marks the qiblah; in Medina, visitors pray at the mosque known as the mosque of the two qiblahs.

fork.setup: you're bowed in prayer, facing Jerusalem. a man at the door calls out that the qiblah is now Mecca. what do you do?

fork.reveal: in Bukhari they turned where they stood, in the middle of the prayer, and carried on.

original.note: Arabic: 'the qiblah', the direction Muslims face in prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims face Mecca; that's all.
what it means: the direction once changed mid-prayer, and the worshipers turned without leaving the prayer.
what a scholar hears: 2:142–150; Bukhari 40 and 403 on the people who turned mid-prayer; the mosque of the two qiblahs is identified by tradition.

sources.quoted: So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:142–144 (the turning of his face to heaven; Allah would not let their faith go to waste; the believers to turn their faces wherever they are)
Sahih al-Bukhari 40 (he loved to face the Ka'bah; a man passes a mosque and they turn mid-prayer)
Sahih al-Bukhari 403 (the people of Quba turn at the dawn prayer)

notes: Pickthall 2:144 phrase quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.
Bukhari 40 and 403 numbers cited from memory; confirm.
Identification of the mosque of the two qiblahs (Banu Salimah) is by tradition; the script says 'tradition remembers'. The Bukhari reports name the mosque the man passed and Quba. Confirm framing.
'The house tradition says Abraham raised': the Qur'an (2:127) says Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations; could cite instead. Confirm.
'The house of worship of the earlier prophets' as a description of Jerusalem; confirm wording.
The myth that earlier prayers were 'wrong' draws on 2:143 (Allah would not make your faith go to waste); confirm the reveal.
